paragraphs: Soon after dinner, the rest of the small party staying with my friend Geoffrey Aldwych had drifted away to play bridge and billiards. He had recently bought a charming old house in a little village north of Sheringham on the Norfolk coast. For the moment, Mrs Aldwych and I were alone in the drawing room, sitting on opposite sides of a small round table that we had been trying, very patiently and unsuccessfully, to make turn. Whatever pressure we had brought to bear, psychic or physical, had been of the friendliest and most encouraging kind. Yet it had not overcome even the slight resistance one might expect from such a small object. The table remained as fixed as the most constant of stars. Not even a tremor passed through its thin, spindle-like legs. After a considerable time spent patiently trying, we had left it to its wooden rest and begun discussing psychic theories instead. At least now there was no stupid table to contradict all our ideas in practice.

I had added that last remark with some bitterness at our failure. If we could not move so insignificant an object, we might as well abandon any hope of moving anything. But the words had barely left my mouth when the abandoned table gave a single, commanding rap, loud and rather startling.
“What’s that?” I asked.
“Only a rap,” she said. “I thought something would happen before long.”
“And do you really think that’s a spirit knocking?” I asked.
“Oh dear, no. I don’t think it has anything at all to do with spirits.”
“Perhaps it has more to do with the very dry weather we’ve been having. Furniture often cracks like that in summer.”

In fact, that was not quite true. In neither summer nor winter have I ever heard furniture crack as that table had. Whatever the sound was, it did not resemble the rough creak of shrinking wood. It was a loud, sharp crack, like one hard object striking another smartly.

“No, I don’t think it had much to do with dry weather either,” she said, smiling. “If you want to know, I think it was the direct result of our attempt to turn the table. Does that sound like nonsense?”
“At present, yes,” I said, “although I’m sure you could make it sound reasonable if you tried. I notice a certain plausibility about you and your theories—”
“Now you’re simply being personal,” she observed.
“For a good reason: to provoke you into explaining and expanding. Please go on.”
“Then let’s walk outside and sit in the garden,” she said, “if you’re sure you prefer my plausible theories to bridge. It’s deliciously warm, and—”
“And darkness will be more suitable for producing psychic phenomena. As at séances,” I said.
“Oh, there’s nothing psychic about my theories,” she said. “According to my theory, the phenomena I mean are purely physical.”

So we wandered into the clear half-light of countless stars. The last crimson feather of sunset, which had hovered in the west for so long, had blown away on the night wind’s breath. The moon would soon rise, but had not yet broken the dim horizon of the sea. The sea lay quiet, breathing gently in its sleep, with a stir of whispering ripples. A little breeze crossed the dark velvet of the closely cut lawn stretching from the house towards the sea. It carried the taste of salt and the freshness of night. Now and then it gave a hint, so subtle as to be almost imperceptible, of its journey across the sleeping fragrance of drowsy garden beds, where white moths hovered in search of night nectar. The house, with its two Elizabethan towers topped by battlements, gleamed with many lit windows. We passed out of sight of it, into the shadow of a box hedge clipped into shapes and monstrous fantasies, and found chairs beside the striped tent at the head of the sheltered outdoor bowling alley.
“And all this is very plausible,” I said. “Now for theories at length, please, and if possible a full-length illustration too.”
“By which you mean a ghost story, or something of the kind?”
“Precisely. And without wishing to dictate, a firsthand one if possible.”
“Strangely enough, I can supply that too,” she said. “First I’ll explain my general theory, then tell you a story that seems to support it. It happened to me, and it happened here.”
“I’m sure it will meet the need,” I said.

She paused while I lit a cigarette, then began in her clear, pleasant voice. Hers is the clearest voice I know. Sitting there in the deeply coloured dusk, I felt that her words were clarity itself. They dropped into the still darkness without any impressions from my other senses to disturb them.

“We are only just beginning to imagine,” she said, “how inseparably mind, soul, life—call it what you like—is woven into the purely material part of the created world. Of course, we have known for centuries that such a connection exists. Doctors knew, for example, that patients recovered better when they were cheerful and optimistic; that fear, the mere emotion, directly affected the heartbeat; that anger caused chemical changes in the blood; that anxiety led to indigestion; and that strong passion could enable a person to do things they are physically incapable of doing in their normal state. Here we have the mind, in simple, familiar ways, producing changes and effects in tissue, in something purely material. Taking this a little further—although it hardly needs taking further at all—we might expect the mind to affect not only what we call living tissue, but also lifeless objects, pieces of wood or stone. At least, it’s hard to see why it should not.”
“Table-turning, for example?” I asked.

“That is one example of how a force from the countless ranks of obscure, mysterious forces stationed within us can pass into material things, as it constantly does. We don’t know the laws governing its passage. Sometimes we want it to pass, and it doesn’t. Just now, when we tried to turn the table, something blocked its path, although I believe the rap afterwards resulted from our efforts. Nothing seems more natural to me than the idea that these forces can be transmitted to lifeless things. We know almost nothing about how they pass, just as we know almost nothing about the actual process by which fear makes the heart beat faster. But just as surely as a Marconi radio message leaps through the air without any visible or solid bridge, these forces can march through some subtle gateway of the body, out of the spirit’s citadel and into material forms. That material may be a living part of ourselves or something we choose to call inanimate nature.”
She paused for a moment.

“In certain circumstances,” she continued, “the force that has passed from us into lifeless things seems able to reveal its presence there. A force entering a table can show itself through the table’s movements or sounds. The table has been charged with physical energy. Time after time, I have seen a table or chair apparently move by itself, but only after it has received some outpouring of force—animal magnetism, call it what you like. To my mind, haunted houses show a similar phenomenon. Usually some crime, or some act involving extreme emotion or passion, has occurred there, and an echo or re-enactment of the deed becomes visible or audible from time to time. Say a murder has taken place and the room is haunted. Psychically sensitive people see the murdered person’s figure there, or, less often, the murderer’s. Cries are heard, or footsteps run back and forth. Somehow the atmosphere has been charged with the scene, and all or part of it repeats itself. We don’t know the laws that govern this, but it is like a phonograph repeating, when properly operated, what has been spoken into it.”
“This is all theory,” I remarked.

“But it seems to account for a curious set of facts, which is all we ask of a theory. Otherwise, we must either openly reject haunted houses altogether or suppose that the murdered person’s spirit, poor wretch, is forced under certain conditions to relive the horror of the body’s tragedy. As though having the body killed there were not enough, the soul must be dragged back and made to live through it again, so vividly that its anguish becomes visible or audible to psychically sensitive people. To me that is unthinkable. My theory is not. Have I made it at all clear?”
“It’s clear enough,” I said, “but I want evidence for it—the full-sized illustration.”
“I promised you one: a ghost story from my own experience.”
Mrs Aldwych paused again, then began the story that was to illustrate her theory.

“It is exactly a year,” she said, “since Jack bought this house from old Mrs Denison. Both of us had heard it was supposed to be haunted, but neither knew any details about the haunting. A month ago, I heard what I believe was the ghost. When Mrs Denison stayed with us last week, I asked exactly what it was and found that it matched my experience completely. I’ll tell you what happened to me first, then give her account of the haunting.

“A month ago, Jack went away for a few days, and I stayed here alone. One Sunday evening I went to bed at about eleven, in my usual health and spirits, as far as I’m aware—both serenely excellent. My room is on the first floor, just at the foot of the stairs to the floor above. There are four other rooms along my passage, all empty that night. At the far end, a door leads onto the landing at the top of the front staircase. Beyond that, as you know, are more bedrooms, also empty that night. In fact, I was the only person sleeping on the first floor.

“The head of my bed is close behind my door, with an electric light above it. A switch at the bedhead controls that light. Another switch there turns on a light in the passage just outside. That was Jack’s idea. If you need to leave your room when the house is dark, you can light the passage before going out instead of fumbling blindly for a switch outside.

“I usually sleep soundly. Once asleep, I very rarely wake before I’m called. But that night I did wake, which was unusual. More unusual still, I woke shuddering with a terror I could not explain. I tried to locate its cause, track it down and reason it away, but nothing worked. Fear of something I could not imagine stared me in the face—white, shaking terror. There was no point lying there trembling in the dark, so I switched on my lamp. To calm this strange disorder of fear, I began reading again in the book I had brought upstairs. It happened to be ‘The Green Carnation,’ a book you would think would do wonders for trembling nerves. But it failed, just as reasoning had failed. After a few pages, with my heart still hammering in my throat and terror’s grip no looser, I switched off the light and lay down again. Before doing so, I looked at my watch. I remember it was ten minutes to two.

“Nothing improved. Terror was slowly becoming a little more definite: terror of some dark, violent deed drawing nearer every moment. It held me in a vice. Something was coming. My subconscious sensed its approach and had already passed that knowledge to my conscious mind. Then the clock gave two jingling chimes, and the stable clock outside clanged the hour more resonantly.

“I still lay there, helpless, my heart pounding. Then I heard a sound just outside my room, on the stairs leading, as I’ve said, to the second floor. It was a perfectly ordinary, unmistakable sound. Feet were feeling their way downstairs in the dark towards my passage. I could also hear a searching hand slipping and sliding along the banister. The footsteps crossed the few yards between the foot of the stairs and my door. Then clothing brushed against the door itself, and fingers blindly felt across its panels. The handle rattled as they passed over it. My terror almost made me scream.

“Then a reasonable hope struck me. Perhaps the midnight wanderer was a servant, ill or needing something. And yet—why the shuffling feet and the groping hand? The instant that hope dawned—for I knew it was the footsteps, and whatever was moving in the dark passage, that frightened me—I switched on both my bedside light and the passage light, opened the door and looked out. The passage was brightly lit from end to end, but completely empty. Yet although I could see no walker, I could still hear one. Along the brightly lit boards, the shuffle grew fainter as it moved away. Judging by the sound, it turned into the gallery at the end and died away. With it, all my terror vanished too. It was It I had feared. Now It and my terror had passed. I went back to bed and slept until morning.”
Again Mrs Aldwych paused, and I said nothing. Somehow the horror lay in the utter simplicity of her experience. Almost at once she continued.

“Now for what followed,” she said, “or what I choose to call the explanation. As I told you, Mrs Denison came to stay not long ago. I mentioned that we had heard, though only vaguely, that the house was supposed to be haunted, and asked her to tell me about it. This is what she said:

“‘In 1610, the heiress to this property was a girl named Helen Denison, engaged to young Lord Southern. If she had children, the property would therefore pass out of the Denison family. If she died childless, it would pass to her first cousin. A week before the wedding, he and one of his brothers rode here from thirty miles away after dark and entered the house. They made their way to her room on the second floor, gagged her, and tried to kill her. But she escaped, felt her way along this passage, and reached the room at the end of the gallery. They followed and killed her there. The facts became known because the younger brother gave evidence for the King against his accomplice.’

“Mrs Denison told me that the ghost has never been seen, but is sometimes heard coming downstairs or passing along the corridor. She said it is heard only between two and three in the morning, the hour in which the murder happened.”
“Have you heard it again since?” I asked.
“Yes, more than once. But it has never frightened me again. Like everyone, I feared what I didn’t know.”
“I think I would fear what I did know, if I knew it was that,” I said.
“I don’t think you would for long. Whatever theory you accept about those footsteps and that searching hand, I can’t see anything to shock or frighten you. You know my own theory—”
“Please apply it to what you heard,” I said.

“It’s simple enough. The poor girl felt her way along this passage in the despair of agonising terror, doubtless hearing her murderers’ soft footsteps gaining on her as she groped along her lost path. The waves of that terrible storm in her brain impressed themselves on the place in some subtle but physical way. Only people we call psychically sensitive could perceive the ripples, so to speak, left in the sand by those breaking waves—and even they could not always perceive them. But they are there, just as the waves are there when a Marconi radio is working, although only a receiver tuned to them can detect them. If you believe in brainwaves at all, the explanation isn’t so difficult.”
“Then the brainwave is permanent?”
“Every wave, of whatever kind, leaves a mark, doesn’t it? If you don’t believe any of this, shall I give you a room along the route of that poor, harmless, murdered walker?”
I stood up.
“I’m very comfortable where I am, thank you,” I said.
